title: Does viscosity protect populations through kinship or through local density?
question: Viscous populations (newborns placed beside their parent) survive longer and breed faster than well-mixed ones (F, F2, L). Is that because newborns start next to a relative, or simply next to someone? A third condition places well-mixed newborns beside a random living agent that is not a recorded relative.
background: L (ticks 0-6000): births per agent-tick 0.0027 well-mixed vs 0.0036 viscous; starvation 37% vs 31% of deaths; killings 58% vs 67%. Food respawns uniformly, so food patches cannot explain it. Interpretation rule, fixed in advance: if only density matters, H26a and H26b are supported and H26c and H26d are not; if only kinship matters, the reverse. Seeds 1100-1111 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: Density: newborns placed beside a stranger survive longer as populations than randomly placed ones
Density: placing newborns beside a stranger raises the early birth rate
Kinship: placing newborns beside their parent beats placing them beside a stranger (survival)
Kinship: placing newborns beside their parent beats placing them beside a stranger (early birth rate)
Fourth test: viscous populations survive longer than well-mixed ones
